records.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
records.summary: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. records.title: Hegseth dodges impeachment after using troops and vets for cover
records.summary: Observers are reporting that absent Democrats likely torpedoed Thomas Massie's attempt to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in the House last night. The vote to refer his eight articles of impeachment to the judiciary committee for a sure death, passed 211-204. Hegseth and his compadres in the Pentagon are no doubt feeling vindicated since he spent Tuesday morning boasting of his handling of the war policies in Yemen, the Caribbean, Venezuela, and in particular, Iran. In order to do this he had to engage in some serious fabrications about the state of the war: that it was "won," that Iran's military is "in ruin," the "ironclad blockade (is) unbroken," that "we control the Strait of Hormuz." It is worth watching in full . "For the first time in American history, a cabinet secretary overseeing America's military is being attacked not for losing conflicts with our enemies, but for winning them," Hegseth declared. records.title: AIPAC dumped more than $55 million into losing midterm races
records.summary: The largest pro-Israel group in the U.S., the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), has been silent on social media since Tuesday afternoon, well before polls closed across the country and Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a blue wave, largely driven by dissatisfaction over rising costs sparked by the war in Iran. The group was an early supporter of the war and a major funder of ads attacking House and Senate candidates calling to cut off aid to Israel. It spent big on the 2026 midterm elections, dumping $84.1 million via its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), and several other PACs into races that have been decided as of this writing. AIPAC might be silent today because they need to explain to their donors how nearly-two-thirds, or $55.3 million, of that spending went to races in which the group’s preferred candidate lost. A failure to achieve the desired results from two-thirds of its political spending will be a tough reality to present to donors, especially when AIPAC repeatedly claims that “being pro-Israel is good policy and good politics.” AIPAC’s failures to deliver results for its donors stands in sharp contrast with the 2022 midterm election,

records.title: Major losses could spur Trump to escalate war before year's end
records.summary: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. records.summary: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) announced Tuesday that they would not back Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in his effort to become majority leader next year. The duo — leading voices on the center and left of the Democratic Party — took pains to avoid discussing specific policy issues, arguing instead that it is time for a new generation of leaders to take charge. "If this campaign was about anything, it was about change," Sanders said, adding that “poll after poll suggests that the American people want bold change.” “The public is done with people who say a lot of words but aren’t actually going to put more money in people’s pockets,” Slotkin said. “I personally will work with anyone who wants to work on that mission instead of looking like we’re doing things.” Neither Sanders nor Slotkin specified who they would support in the race for majority leader, though Slotkin said she had a “productive conversation” with Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Mary.) about his potential candidacy. The joint press conference suggests that momentum is building behind the effort to find new Democratic leadership in the Senate. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. records.summary: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. records.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
records.summary: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). This decision comes down to issues that have little to do with the act itself, nor even really with trade between the United States and these countries. Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. The preferential trade agreement — originally signed into law in 2000 by President Bill Clinton and most recently renewed in September for two additional years — provides duty-free access for over 7,000 goods to the U.S. market for qualifying sub-Saharan countries. In exchange for this preferential access, AGOA requires countries to meet a set of vague requirements, including reducing barriers to American exporters, ensuring governance and human rights standards, and not posing a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interest

records.summary: It has long been claimed that Americans do not vote based on foreign policy, but the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections demonstrated the limits of this truism, with a large majority of voters rejecting the Iran War waged by the Trump administration. Even before the election, an October Fox News poll indicated that the Iran war and issues associated with it (inflation and gas prices) were among the top issues voters were concerned about. Exit polling published by NBC News showed 74% of voters saw the Iran war as a “crucial” or “major factor” in their vote, while 62% believed using force against Iran was the wrong decision. This apparently has come as a nasty surprise to the war’s biggest defenders and surrogates, who had assured their followers that this backlash would not happen. Some have admitted their errors, but many have not, and that split has rapidly produced a circular firing squad, with neocons aggressively turning on those in their ranks who have conceded the war was a mistake. records.summary: If foreign policy could decide an election, then 1992 upended expectations. Bush found himself reminding Americans that he had led the USSR peacefully into history’s dustbin while also liberating Kuwait from the clutches of Saddam Hussein. “My opponents say I spend too much time on foreign policy, as if it didn't matter that schoolchildren once hid under their desks in drills to prepare for nuclear war,” said Bush during his acceptance speech at the 1992 Republican National Convention. “Over the past 4 years, more people have breathed the fresh air of freedom than in all of human history.” Foreign policy mattered to Bush. He was a combat pilot during the Second World War and later served as ambassador to the United Nations, CIA Director, and Ronald Reagan’s vice president. It mattered a lot less to voters angry about a sluggish economy and high unemployment: 73% said the country was on the wrong track in 1992. records.title: Nvidia Lacks Corporate D&O Insurance Amid Huang Scandal
records.summary: Nvidia Lacks Corporate D&O Insurance Amid Huang Scandal Nvidia does not have directors’ and officers’ (D&O) liability insurance covering the company itself, an unusual omission for a major US-listed corporation that could leave the chipmaker facing substantial legal costs amid the controversy surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang, according to Financial Times . The FT writes that while Nvidia reportedly maintains $900mn in insurance protecting its directors and senior executives from personal liability, the policy does not extend to the company’s own financial exposure. The coverage, arranged through Aon and involving insurers including Beazley, AIG and Chubb, is limited to what the industry calls Side A protection. Most large publicly traded US companies also purchase Side B and Side C insurance, which can reimburse corporate legal expenses and cover certain claims brought directly against the company. Nvidia’s decision to operate without these protections is uncommon, although high premiums can lead some businesses to retain such risks themselves. records.title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this
records.summary: Ulster Hall, Belfast With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers ‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage. They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever. Continue reading...

records.summary: America's Top Beef Processor Sees "Worst Part" Of Cattle Cycle Over One of America's largest beef processors has spotted an inflection point in the industry's brutal multiyear margin squeeze, saying the " worst part of the cycle" is over as cattle futures and supermarket ground beef prices retreat from their highs. "We do believe we are through the worst part of the cycle ," National Beef CEO Tim Klein told reporters on Thursday, Bloomberg reported. Klein pointed out that reduced US slaughter volumes helped improve processing margins, while robust consumer demand supported elevated beef prices. The Missouri-based company, controlled by Brazil's MBRF Global Foods SA, reported an earnings margin before items including interest and taxes of 2.1%, its highest since 3Q24 . National Beef's earnings results follow improving earnings at JBS NV's US beef business, potentially showing more evidence that margin pressure across the industry could be easing. records.title: ‘All I could smell was fertiliser’: the best (and worst) supermarket instant coffee, tasted and rated
records.summary: Our coffee snob spills the beans on which granules hint at chocolate and caramel, and which leave a bitter note • Everything you need to make great coffee I’m a coffee snob with my own grinder, but I found the haptic thwack, whack and crack of opening the lid and film on a jar of instant coffee strangely invigorating, and rather nostalgic. When I took a deep sniff, however, disaster: all I could smell was fertiliser! Instant coffee is brewed at scorching temperatures, then either freeze-dried in a vacuum or spray-dried using hot air. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. This gives it an earthier, muskier and more bitter flavour profile, though, thankfully, with a little alchemy and hot water, those more familiar coffee aromas and flavours returned, with notes of chicory, bitter chocolate and burnt sugar. Almost all of these products have a similar industrial imprint, uniform granules and a one-dimensional flavour profile, so they’re ultimately more a simulation of the real thing. records.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for sauteed cabbage with cheese cream and sunflower seeds
records.summary: A rich, comforting plateful of sweet, crunchy hispi topped with a cheesy cream – like a bowl of pasta, only without the carbs This is a fun recipe that takes advantage of the hispi cabbage’s sweet nature and pliant structure. You can give it a really hard blast of heat, and it will crisp, caramelise and smoke, but still retain a lot of its easy freshness and bright crunch; it will also take on a pleasing, slightly slippery texture, like buttered noodles. This plate has the satisfaction of a hearty bowl of pasta without being nearly so enervating, and it works fantastically as a side dish, too, either as a companion to toasted whole grains or some grilled mushrooms. records.title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters
records.summary: Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence ( The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November ). The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences. Continue reading...

records.title: Three cheers for Melania Trump-led ceasefire in Ukraine
records.summary: The humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine, mediated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV and jointly implemented by Ukraine and Russia, is unprecedented since the start of this war in 2022. Its success and people-centered spirit also stand in conspicuous contrast to the repeated attempts by the Trump administration to end the war, which have all ended in frustrated failure. There has been pragmatic, if intermittent, engagement between Russia and Ukraine virtually since the 2022 Russian invasion, around issues like the exchange of prisoners of war and the bodies of the fallen, or the Black Sea Grain Initiative . But until October 27, 2026, no humanitarian ceasefire along the frontline had ever been successfully implemented; it had never even been attempted. The story of how Oleshky became a step on the path towards peace has twists and turns. The town on the left bank of the Dnieper River was occupied on the first day of the 2022 Russian invasion. records.summary: From Sabotaged Supermarkets To RAF Fairford: Iran's War On Europe Is No Longer Deniable Authored by Struan Stevenson via Townhall , France has finally done what European governments have been reluctant to do for far too long. On November 10, Paris formally accused the Iranian regime of conducting cyberwarfare against French citizens, attributing attacks on more than 700 supermarket sites to an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The consequences were extraordinary. Hackers manipulated refrigeration systems, destroying food worth tens of millions of euros and causing fires. This was not ordinary cybercrime. It was state-sponsored industrial sabotage on French soil. But the latest revelations are even more alarming. The United States Department of Justice has now unveiled an indictment alleging that Iran-backed operatives orchestrated a terrorist plot against RAF Fairford , the British airbase housing American military personnel and aircraft. records.summary: Why Most Americans Couldn't Last 72 Hours In An Emergency Authored by Russ Jones via The Epoch Times , Viral social media posts and text messages urging Americans to stockpile 90 days of food and supplies are gaining traction. One text message, reviewed by The Epoch Times, spread as these warnings usually do: from one friend to the next. It described a cyber specialist who came home from a conference shaken enough to warn people close to him to keep 90 days of provisions for every member of their household. According to the message, the concern was Iran, its cyber capabilities, and what might follow the Nov. 3 midterm elections. It named no verifiable sources. "I'm not trying to incite panic, nor create a run on toilet paper," the message read. "I'm not a 'sky is falling' person, but I'll be ready." For Americans who have spent years quietly filling pantries, warnings like that are nothing new. However, they say this latest alarm seemed to echo something the federal government actually said. records.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
records.summary: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

records.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
records.summary: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. records.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
records.summary: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. Less than 1% of Americans serve in the military. records.title: AIPAC dumped more than $55 million into losing midterm races
records.summary: The largest pro-Israel group in the U.S., the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), has been silent on social media since Tuesday afternoon, well before polls closed across the country and Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a blue wave, largely driven by dissatisfaction over rising costs sparked by the war in Iran. The group was an early supporter of the war and a major funder of ads attacking House and Senate candidates calling to cut off aid to Israel. It spent big on the 2026 midterm elections, dumping $84.1 million via its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), and several other PACs into races that have been decided as of this writing. AIPAC might be silent today because they need to explain to their donors how nearly-two-thirds, or $55.3 million, of that spending went to races in which the group’s preferred candidate lost. records.title: Major losses could spur Trump to escalate war before year's end
records.summary: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. records.title: Are Democrats ready to make the most of the blue wave?
records.summary: Unless you’ve been living under a rock (no shame Patrick Star!), you’ve likely heard about last Tuesday’s “Blue Wave” midterm elections . The Democrats’ strong performance at the polls flipped control of the House and the Senate, delivering stunning results on the way, including flipping long-time red states like Kansas and Texas. As the GOP scrambles to repair the damage and Democrats strategize about how to use their new power in a divided Washington, one takeaway seems obvious: this was a foreign policy election, in which the Iran war and the costs it brought home served as the tipping point. But can we read these election results as a repudiation of U.S. foreign policy writ-large, or is this a specific response to one of the dumbest interventions in the long history of American adventurism? What does JD Vance's day-after effort to distance himself from the war tell us about how Republicans are digesting this result? And if Tuesday was a rebuke of U.S. foreign policy as usual, are Democrats ready to respond accordingly? records.summary: After Democrats dominated last week’s midterm elections, retaking control of the House and Senate, President Donald Trump has turned his attention southward. “Cuba is falling. It’s a failing nation. It’s got an ideology very similar to what the Democrat ideology is,” he said Monday. “I would imagine it will fall fairly soon.” The comments suggest that, despite facing a stunning rebuke of his foreign-policy adventurism in Iran, Trump is not quite ready to give up on his goal, reiterated as recently as last month, of overthrowing the Cuban government. So is Trump poised to go beyond economic pressure and saber rattling by launching a military campaign against Cuba? The answer is “no” — or at least “not yet.” Many analysts predict that a lame-duck president constrained by domestic setbacks could seek redemption through foreign-policy achievements, including by lashing out at seemingly easier targets like an impoverished Caribbean nation. records.title: 'Junk history' and Swedish neutrality
records.summary: The historian Stephen Kotkin of Stanford’s Hoover Institution has penned an important new essay on the phenomenon of “junk history”: reductionist or plainly wrong interpretations of historical events that have little or no basis in empirical reality but are nevertheless “marshaled in policy debates as justification for action, up to launching wars.” The emblematic example, which has recently been used by advocates for the war with Iran, is the failure of British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain to truly ensure “peace in our time” at Munich in 1938. As Kotkin once put it, “It turns out not everything is Munich. records.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
records.summary: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). This decision comes down to issues that have little to do with the act itself, nor even really with trade between the United States and these countries. Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. The preferential trade agreement — originally signed into law in 2000 by President Bill Clinton and most recently renewed in September for two additional years — provides duty-free access for over 7,000 goods to the U.S. market for qualifying sub-Saharan countries. A CIA officer from the Munich Operations Base was in charge. The Hungarian crewmen he had recruited stood nearby in flight suits. With them were two Ukrainian exiles who had volunteered to parachute into their homeland. They were code-named Apostle 1 and Apostle 2. Each carried forged identity papers, a miniature radio transmitter, a pistol, a machine gun, hand grenades, a purse full of gold coins, and a poison pill to be taken in case of capture. An unmarked C-47 transport plane was waiting. The CIA officer overseeing this operation, a twenty-six-year-old Yale graduate named Stephen Tanner, watched the plane take off and disappear into the night. It flew over East Germany and Poland, then crossed into Soviet airspace. As it approached the Ukrainian city of Lviv, a cargo bay swung open. The two Ukrainians jumped into the darkness. records.title: Kushner & Witkoff do the Abu Dhabi shuffle: Ukraine peace ahead?
records.summary: The talks in Abu Dhabi demonstrate that the Ukraine peace process is finally moving in the right direction. Whether it will reach its goal is of course another matter. Firstly, the U.S. negotiating team has introduced to the talks the critical issue of a future European security architecture. President Trump has written of the need for a "very big, beautiful agreement that might involve all of Europe." As Jared Kushner wrote before the talks: “For more than 30 years, Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework. Decades of mistrust, competing security concerns, and the devastating consequences of this war make this an extraordinarily difficult challenge, but one that is essential to lasting peace. Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment. records.title: Democrats not yet unified for first big post-election Iran war test
records.summary: Congressional Democrats will face the first test of their willingness to translate their electoral gains into action against the Iran war before the new Congress is seated in January. While almost all Democrats appear united in wanting to end the war, a question of how to do so — and, perhaps more importantly, when to do so — is looming. Some are urging the current Congress to target Dec. 11, when ongoing government spending authority runs out. Though Democrats will still be in the minority at that point, activists and a number of members argue that the midterm results give the party both the political capital and the leverage needed to act. “I’m not interested in continuing to throw a blank check to Pete Hegseth for a war the American people never authorized,” Rep. Chris DeLuzio (D-Pa.) told reporters on Wednesday. “That’s on the Republicans. They have full control of this Congress until January. records.title: Ukraine is running out of time
records.summary: After over four-and-a-half years of entrenched warfare, reports of U.S.-backed peace talks to end Russia's war on Ukraine are back in the news. After Finland and Norway held Europe’s first direct talks with President Vladimir Putin in a year, more trilateral talks between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia are planned for later this month. While we’ve heard tales of imminent peace time and again, here's hoping American emissaries and their counterparts can finally bring an end to the fighting.That’s because, despite considerable efforts by the U.S. and Europe to help Ukraine win this war, there is no victory in sight. While Ukrainians arguably thwarted Russian advances in its very first weeks, its backers have failed to help Ukraine consolidate its battlefield victories at the negotiating table. As a result, Russia’s invasion has slowly wrecked Ukraine: the war is Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II and Russia has seized approximately a fifth of Ukraine’s territory . After years of needless death and destruction, what will it take to actually forge an agreement to finally end this war? records.title: Election was a check on Trump — and Biden — foreign policy
records.summary: There is no debate as to why Donald Trump and the Republican Party suffered a historic and humiliating defeat at the polls on Tuesday: it all comes down to the Iran war and the cost-of-living crisis it has brought about. But lost in the conversation is that this was not just a rejection of the Iran war. It was also a repudiation of the broader foreign policy that repeatedly gets the U.S. into wars — or into supporting the wars and war crimes of U.S. partners. In many contests on Tuesday, the U.S.-Israel relationship was on the ballot too, and it was rejected by Republicans and Democrats alike in favor of recentering priorities back to national interests, including ending the flow of military aid to Israel. Trump famously ran on a promise to end forever wars and not to start new ones. But he ended up listening to the Israeli Prime Minister and started a major war with Iran, even though a diplomatic deal was on the table that was objectively stronger than President Barack Obama’s deal . Trump could have declared victory, but instead he listened to the Israeli government and chose to declare war. Now he is paying for it by losing his majority in Congress. records.title: Neocons in full meltdown as voters punish GOP for Iran war
records.summary: It has long been claimed that Americans do not vote based on foreign policy, but the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections demonstrated the limits of this truism, with a large majority of voters rejecting the Iran War waged by the Trump administration. Even before the election, an October Fox News poll indicated that the Iran war and issues associated with it (inflation and gas prices) were among the top issues voters were concerned about. Exit polling published by NBC News showed 74% of voters saw the Iran war as a “crucial” or “major factor” in their vote, while 62% believed using force against Iran was the wrong decision. This apparently has come as a nasty surprise to the war’s biggest defenders and surrogates, who had assured their followers that this backlash would not happen. Some have admitted their errors, but many have not, and that split has rapidly produced a circular firing squad, with neocons aggressively turning on those in their ranks who have conceded the war was a mistake. records.title: 2026 wasn't the first time war swayed an election
records.summary: If foreign policy could decide an election, then 1992 upended expectations. Barely eight months after the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin for the last time, President George H. W. Bush found himself reminding Americans that he had led the USSR peacefully into history’s dustbin while also liberating Kuwait from the clutches of Saddam Hussein. “My opponents say I spend too much time on foreign policy, as if it didn't matter that schoolchildren once hid under their desks in drills to prepare for nuclear war,” said Bush during his acceptance speech at the 1992 Republican National Convention. “Over the past 4 years, more people have breathed the fresh air of freedom than in all of human history.” Foreign policy mattered to Bush. He was a combat pilot during the Second World War and later served as ambassador to the United Nations, CIA Director, and Ronald Reagan’s vice president. It mattered a lot less to voters angry about a sluggish economy and high unemployment: 73% said the country was on the wrong track in 1992. methodology.reliability: A official primary source/catalogue; B established newsroom or independent research; C specialist, advocacy or aggregator; D alternative commentary; E unverified social/community; U unclassified. Grade describes source class, not the truth of a specific claim.
methodology.confidence: Claim confidence is left unassessed unless an upstream collector supplies a numeric value. Source grade is not claim confidence.
methodology.corroboration: The six views reuse the existing archive. Similar stories, repeated posts, syndicated copy or multiple outlets quoting one origin are not independent corroboration. A human must inspect provenance.
methodology.geolocation: Location is shown only when supplied by the source or upstream archive. No location is inferred from a headline.
methodology.limits: This is open-source situational awareness, not intelligence agency coverage, an emergency warning service, a live market terminal or a verified threat assessment.
